walkthroughs.body_html:
Motion, Forces & Energy — a core area of GCSE Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Motion, Forces & Energy brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Motion, Forces & Energy.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A 2 kg object accelerates at 4 m/s². What is the resultant force?
options: 2 N
8 N
6 N

mcqs.q: What does it mean if the resultant force on an object is zero?
options: The object must be stationary.
The object is either stationary or moving at constant velocity.
The object is decelerating.
The object is accelerating.

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.

mcqs.q: When energy is 'lost' as heat due to friction, what has really happened?
options: Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Energy has been transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings — it's not destroyed, just dissipated.
Energy has been used up and no longer exists.

mcqs.q: If a car doubles its speed, what happens to its kinetic energy?
options: It quadruples (because KE = 1/2 mv^2 — kinetic energy is proportional to v^2).
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.
Kinetic energy doubles because energy is proportional to speed.
